questions.stem: A DynamoDB table uses an order status attribute, with values such as PENDING and SHIPPED, as its partition key. Most traffic goes to a few partitions and requests are throttled. What should the developer change?

options.text: Switch every read to strongly consistent
options.rationale: Consistency does not change how traffic is spread across partitions.

options.text: Use a high-cardinality attribute, such as order ID, as the partition key
options.rationale: Many distinct key values spread requests evenly across partitions.

options.text: Add a local secondary index that uses the status attribute as its sort key
options.rationale: An LSI shares the table's partition key, so the hot partitions remain.

options.text: Use Scan instead of Query to read orders
options.rationale: Scans read the whole table and use more capacity.

questions.explanation: A partition key with few values creates hot partitions; choose a key with many distinct values.

questions.stem: Right after updating an item in a DynamoDB table, an application reads the item back and sometimes gets the old value. The read must always return the latest data. What should the developer do?

options.text: Query a global secondary index with strongly consistent reads
options.rationale: Global secondary indexes support only eventually consistent reads.

options.text: Add a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster in front of the table
options.rationale: DAX serves eventually consistent reads from its cache.

options.text: Set ConsistentRead to true on the GetItem request
options.rationale: A strongly consistent read reflects all writes that succeeded before the read.

options.text: Increase the table's read capacity
options.rationale: More capacity does not change the consistency model.

questions.explanation: Reads are eventually consistent by default; request a strongly consistent read when the latest value is required.

questions.stem: A DynamoDB table holds orders for many customers. An application must retrieve one customer's orders without reading the rest of the table. Which approaches will do this? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Scan the table with a projection expression
options.rationale: A projection limits the attributes returned, not the items read.

options.text: Query a global secondary index keyed on customer ID
options.rationale: A GSI lets you query efficiently on an attribute that is not the table's key.

options.text: Run a parallel scan on the table
options.rationale: Parallel scans finish faster but still read the whole table.

options.text: Query the table when customer ID is its partition key
options.rationale: Query reads only the items with that partition key value.

options.text: Scan the table with a filter expression on customer ID
options.rationale: A scan reads every item; the filter only trims what is returned.

questions.explanation: Query reads by key; Scan reads everything. Design keys and indexes so access patterns use Query.

questions.stem: An existing DynamoDB table uses user ID as its partition key. The application now also needs to look up users by email address. What should the developer add?

options.text: A new local secondary index that uses email as its sort key
options.rationale: Local secondary indexes can only be created along with the table and keep the same partition key.

options.text: A filter expression on a Scan of the table
options.rationale: Scans read the whole table for every lookup.

options.text: A DynamoDB stream on the table
options.rationale: Streams record item changes; they do not enable new queries.

options.text: A global secondary index with email as its partition key
options.rationale: GSIs can be added to existing tables and use a different partition key.

questions.explanation: A new lookup key on an existing table calls for a global secondary index, which can be added later and has its own partition key. A local secondary index is the nearest distractor, but it can only be created with the table and keeps the table's partition key.

questions.stem: Session items in a DynamoDB table should be removed automatically a set time after they are created, without extra write costs. What should the developer use?

options.text: Time to Live (TTL), with an expiry timestamp attribute on each item
options.rationale: DynamoDB deletes expired items in the background without using write capacity.

options.text: A scheduled Lambda function that scans for and deletes expired items
options.rationale: This works but costs read and write capacity and needs code to maintain.

options.text: An Amazon S3 Lifecycle rule on the table
options.rationale: Lifecycle rules apply to S3 objects, not DynamoDB items.

options.text: A conditional write on each new item
options.rationale: Condition expressions control whether a write happens, not when an item expires.

questions.explanation: TTL takes an epoch timestamp attribute and removes items after that time.

questions.stem: Application logs are written to an Amazon S3 bucket. They must move to a cheaper archive storage class after 90 days and be deleted after one year. Which actions should the developer configure? (Select TWO.)

options.text: S3 Versioning on the bucket
options.rationale: Versioning keeps earlier versions; it does not move or delete objects by age.

options.text: S3 Object Lock in compliance mode, with a retention period set to one year
options.rationale: Object Lock prevents deletion during retention and does not move objects to another storage class.

options.text: An S3 Lifecycle expiration action at 365 days
options.rationale: Expiration actions make S3 delete objects once they reach a set age.

options.text: A DynamoDB TTL attribute on each log file
options.rationale: TTL applies to DynamoDB items, not S3 objects.

options.text: An S3 Lifecycle transition to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval at 90 days
options.rationale: Transition actions move objects to another storage class once they reach a set age.

questions.explanation: One Lifecycle rule can hold a transition action (change storage class by age) and an expiration action (delete by age). Object Lock is the nearest distractor, but it prevents deletion and never moves objects.

questions.stem: An application stores user-uploaded videos that can be several gigabytes each. The data must be highly durable and served to users by URL. Which data store fits this access pattern?

options.text: Amazon DynamoDB
options.rationale: DynamoDB items have a small maximum size, so large files are usually kept in S3.

options.text: Amazon ElastiCache
options.rationale: ElastiCache is an in-memory cache, not durable storage for large files.

options.text: Amazon S3
options.rationale: S3 stores large objects durably and serves them over HTTPS.

options.text: Amazon RDS, with the videos in a binary column
options.rationale: Storing large binaries in a relational database is costly and slow to serve.

questions.explanation: Large objects go in S3; databases hold metadata and a pointer to the object.

questions.stem: A read-heavy application uses DynamoDB and needs microsecond read latency for repeated reads of the same items, with as few code changes as possible. Which caching solution fits?

options.text: Amazon ElastiCache with lazy loading code
options.rationale: This works but needs cache-management logic written into the application.

options.text: Amazon CloudFront in front of the table
options.rationale: CloudFront caches HTTP content at edge locations, not DynamoDB API calls.

options.text: An Amazon RDS read replica
options.rationale: Read replicas apply to relational databases, not DynamoDB.

options.text: DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX)
options.rationale: DAX is an in-memory cache for DynamoDB that is API-compatible, so code changes are small.

questions.explanation: The clues are DynamoDB, microsecond repeated reads and few code changes: DAX is an API-compatible cache for DynamoDB. ElastiCache is the nearest distractor; it works, but the application must add its own cache-management code.

questions.stem: An application caches database query results in Amazon ElastiCache by using lazy loading. After records are updated, users sometimes see old data. Which changes will reduce stale reads? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Read from a database read replica instead of the primary
options.rationale: Replicas can lag, and the cache would still hold stale entries.

options.text: Set a time to live (TTL) on cached entries
options.rationale: Entries expire and are reloaded, which limits how long stale data can be served.

options.text: Use a larger cache node type
options.rationale: More memory holds more entries but does not make them fresher.

options.text: Turn off cache eviction
options.rationale: Keeping entries longer increases staleness.

options.text: Update or delete the cached entry on each write
options.rationale: Refreshing or removing the entry when the record changes keeps the cache in step with the database.

questions.explanation: Lazy loading only refreshes on a miss; add TTLs or write-through updates to limit stale data.

questions.stem: Logs in an Amazon CloudWatch Logs log group grow without limit. The company needs only the last 30 days. What is the simplest way to keep only 30 days of logs?

options.text: Set the log group's retention period to 30 days
options.rationale: CloudWatch Logs deletes events older than the retention setting automatically.

options.text: Create an S3 Lifecycle rule for the log group
options.rationale: Lifecycle rules apply to S3 buckets, not log groups.

options.text: Write a scheduled function that deletes old log streams
options.rationale: This needs code and does not remove older events inside active streams.

options.text: Add a DynamoDB TTL attribute to each log event
options.rationale: TTL is a DynamoDB feature.

questions.explanation: Log groups keep data forever by default until you set a retention period.

questions.stem: An application writes an item to a DynamoDB table and immediately queries a global secondary index for it. The query sometimes misses the new item, and setting ConsistentRead to true on the query returns an error. What is the reason?

options.text: The table's provisioned read capacity is too low for the query's traffic
options.rationale: Low capacity causes throttling errors, not missing items.

options.text: Global secondary indexes do not support strongly consistent reads
options.rationale: Updates reach a GSI asynchronously, and strongly consistent reads are not available on GSIs.

options.text: The index projects the key attributes and no others
options.rationale: The projection decides which attributes come back, not whether a new item is visible.

options.text: The query uses a scan instead of a key condition expression
options.rationale: The scenario describes a query on the index.

questions.explanation: Strongly consistent reads work on tables and local secondary indexes; GSIs are eventually consistent.

questions.stem: Two users edit the same document item in a DynamoDB table at the same time, and one user's changes silently overwrite the other's. How can the developer detect this conflict?

options.text: Read the item with strong consistency right before each update
options.rationale: Fresh reads do not stop a later write from overwriting a concurrent one.

options.text: Enable DynamoDB Streams on the table
options.rationale: Streams record changes after they happen; they do not block conflicting writes.

options.text: Add a version attribute and make each update conditional on it
options.rationale: The second write fails its condition, so the application knows the item changed since it was read.

options.text: Increase the table's write capacity
options.rationale: Capacity does not affect which write wins.

questions.explanation: Optimistic locking uses a version attribute and a condition expression on each write.

questions.stem: An application moves points between two users' items in a DynamoDB table. Either both items must be updated, or neither. What should the developer use?

options.text: BatchWriteItem with both updates
options.rationale: Batch writes are not atomic; one write can succeed while the other fails.

options.text: Two UpdateItem calls with exponential backoff
options.rationale: Retries do not undo the first update if the second one fails.

options.text: A conditional write on the first of the two items
options.rationale: This protects one item but does not tie the two updates together.

options.text: TransactWriteItems with both updates
options.rationale: A transaction applies all of its writes or none of them.

questions.explanation: DynamoDB transactions give all-or-nothing changes across items.

questions.stem: A DynamoDB Query for one customer's orders returns only part of the results, and the response includes a LastEvaluatedKey. How should the code get the remaining items?

options.text: Repeat the query with ExclusiveStartKey set to LastEvaluatedKey
options.rationale: Each response is one page of up to 1 MB; the key marks where the next page starts.

options.text: Repeat the query with ConsistentRead set to true
options.rationale: Consistency does not change the page size.

options.text: Switch to a Scan operation
options.rationale: Scans are paginated the same way and read far more data.

options.text: Increase the table's provisioned read capacity and repeat the query
options.rationale: Pagination comes from the per-response size limit, not from capacity.

questions.explanation: Query and Scan results are paginated; LastEvaluatedKey and ExclusiveStartKey walk the pages.

questions.stem: A job scans a large DynamoDB table with a filter expression and returns only a few items, yet it consumes a lot of read capacity. Why?

options.text: Filter expressions use strongly consistent reads, which cost twice as much
options.rationale: Consistency is set separately and is not the cause.

options.text: Filters run after items are read, and capacity counts every item read
options.rationale: Filter expressions reduce what is returned, not what is read.

options.text: The filter expression is evaluated once for each attribute in the table
options.rationale: Capacity depends on the data read, not on attribute count.

options.text: A scan reads each item twice, once to filter and once to return it
options.rationale: A scan reads each item once.

questions.explanation: Use key conditions on a table or index to limit what is read; filters only trim the results.

questions.stem: A game needs a real-time leaderboard that updates player scores constantly and returns the top 100 players in order, with very low latency. Which solution is the best fit?

options.text: A DynamoDB table scanned and sorted on each request
options.rationale: Scanning and sorting the whole table on every request is slow and costly.

options.text: Objects in Amazon S3, one per player
options.rationale: S3 has no way to rank objects by a value.

options.text: A sorted set in Amazon ElastiCache
options.rationale: Sorted sets keep members ordered by score and return ranges such as the top 100 quickly.

options.text: An Amazon RDS table queried with ORDER BY on every request
options.rationale: It works at small scale, but constant updates and sorting add load and latency compared with an in-memory sorted set.

questions.explanation: In-memory sorted sets are the standard pattern for leaderboards.

questions.stem: A web application runs on several EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. Users are signed out whenever the Auto Scaling group replaces an instance, because sessions are stored in instance memory. What should the developer do?

options.text: Turn on sticky sessions on the load balancer
options.rationale: Sticky sessions route users to the same instance, but sessions are still lost when it is replaced.

options.text: Store sessions on each instance's EBS volume
options.rationale: The volume belongs to one instance and goes away with it.

options.text: Increase the instances' memory
options.rationale: More memory does not keep sessions when an instance is terminated.

options.text: Store session data in Amazon ElastiCache
options.rationale: A shared session store keeps sessions available to every instance and survives instance replacement.

questions.explanation: Move session state out of the instances into a shared store such as ElastiCache or DynamoDB.

questions.stem: A new application stores orders, customers and invoices. It needs joins across these tables, multi-row transactions and ad hoc reporting queries written in SQL. Which data store fits these access patterns?

options.text: Amazon Aurora
options.rationale: A relational database supports joins, transactions and ad hoc SQL.

options.text: Amazon DynamoDB
options.rationale: DynamoDB is designed for known key-based access patterns and does not support joins.

options.text: Amazon ElastiCache
options.rationale: An in-memory cache is not a durable system of record for relational data.

options.text: Amazon S3
options.rationale: S3 stores objects; it does not provide relational transactions or joins.

questions.explanation: Pick the data store by access pattern: relational queries and joins point to Amazon RDS or Aurora.

questions.stem: Reporting queries on an Amazon Aurora MySQL database slow down the application's writes on the primary instance. Which combination of steps will reduce the load on the primary? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Increase the storage allocated to the primary instance
options.rationale: Aurora storage grows automatically, and more storage does not move read queries off the primary.

options.text: Add one or more Aurora Replicas to the cluster
options.rationale: Replicas serve read traffic from the same shared storage.

options.text: Point the reporting queries at the cluster endpoint
options.rationale: The cluster endpoint connects to the primary instance, which is the instance under load.

options.text: Increase the backup retention period
options.rationale: Backups do not change query load.

options.text: Point the reporting queries at the cluster's reader endpoint
options.rationale: The reader endpoint spreads read connections across the replicas.

questions.explanation: Offload reads to replicas and connect to them through the reader endpoint.

questions.stem: Audit records stored in Amazon S3 must not be deleted or overwritten by anyone, including administrators, for seven years. What should the developer configure?

options.text: An S3 Lifecycle rule that expires objects after seven years
options.rationale: Lifecycle rules delete objects on a schedule; they do not stop earlier deletion.

options.text: S3 Object Lock in compliance mode, with a seven-year retention period
options.rationale: Compliance mode prevents any user from deleting or overwriting a protected version until the retention period ends.

options.text: S3 Object Lock in governance mode, with a seven-year retention period
options.rationale: Users with special permissions can override governance mode.

options.text: S3 Versioning on the bucket, so that earlier versions are kept
options.rationale: Versioning keeps old versions, but users with permission can still delete them.

questions.explanation: Object Lock compliance mode enforces write-once-read-many retention that no user can override.

questions.stem: An application stores customer orders in DynamoDB. It must fetch one customer's orders placed between two dates, efficiently. Which combination of steps will meet this requirement? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use order date as the partition key
options.rationale: Date-based partition keys concentrate traffic and do not group a customer's orders.

options.text: Store each customer's orders in a single item as a list
options.rationale: Items have a size limit, and the list cannot be queried by date range.

options.text: Query with a key condition on the customer ID and a BETWEEN range on the order date
options.rationale: The query reads only the items in that date range.

options.text: Scan the table with a filter on customer ID and date
options.rationale: A scan reads the whole table.

options.text: Use customer ID as the partition key and order date as the sort key
options.rationale: Items for one customer are stored together and sorted by date.

questions.explanation: A sort key lets a query read a range of items within one partition.

questions.stem: An application overwrites an existing object in Amazon S3 and immediately reads it back. What does the read return?

options.text: Possibly the old version, for a few seconds after the write
options.rationale: This was true of S3 in the past, but S3 is now strongly consistent.

options.text: An error, until S3 finishes replicating the object
options.rationale: Reads succeed right away and return the latest version.

options.text: The new version, because S3 is strongly consistent
options.rationale: S3 provides strong read-after-write consistency for PUT and DELETE requests.

options.text: The old version, unless the bucket has versioning turned on
options.rationale: Versioning keeps older versions; it does not affect consistency.

questions.explanation: S3 reads after a successful write or delete return the latest data.

questions.stem: A team needs an in-memory cache that supports data structures such as sorted sets and hashes, replication to a standby, and automatic failover. Which choice fits?

options.text: Amazon ElastiCache with Memcached
options.rationale: Memcached supports simple key-value data without sorted sets or hashes, and node-based Memcached clusters have no replication or automatic failover.

options.text: Amazon S3 with a short Lifecycle expiration rule
options.rationale: S3 is object storage, not an in-memory cache.

options.text: An Amazon EBS volume shared between instances
options.rationale: Block storage is not a cache and does not provide these data structures.

options.text: Amazon ElastiCache with Valkey or Redis OSS
options.rationale: These engines support rich data structures, replication and automatic failover.

questions.explanation: Pick Valkey or Redis OSS for data structures, replication and failover; Memcached for simple multithreaded caching.

questions.stem: A new DynamoDB table uses customer ID as the partition key and order ID as the sort key. The application also needs to query each customer's orders sorted by order date, with strongly consistent reads. The table has not been created yet. What should the developer add?

options.text: A local secondary index on order date, created with the table
options.rationale: An LSI keeps the table's partition key, adds another sort key and supports strongly consistent reads.

options.text: A global secondary index with order date as its partition key
options.rationale: GSIs do not support strongly consistent reads, and a date partition key does not group a customer's orders.

options.text: A local secondary index added after the table is in use
options.rationale: Local secondary indexes can be defined only when the table is created.

options.text: A scan with a filter on customer ID, sorted in the application
options.rationale: A scan reads the whole table and is slow and costly.

questions.explanation: LSIs share the table's partition key, must be created with the table and allow strongly consistent reads.

questions.stem: A new feature stores user profile data and looks it up by user ID millions of times a day, with single-digit millisecond latency at any scale. There are no joins or complex queries. Which data store fits best?

options.text: Amazon RDS for MySQL on a large instance
options.rationale: A relational database can do lookups, but scaling it for this load takes more work, and its features go unused.

options.text: Amazon DynamoDB
options.rationale: DynamoDB serves key-value lookups at consistent low latency at any scale, without server management.

options.text: Amazon S3 with one object per user
options.rationale: S3 is object storage with higher per-request latency than a key-value database.

options.text: Amazon EFS mounted on each application server
options.rationale: A shared file system is not built for key lookups at this scale.

questions.explanation: Simple key-value access at scale points to DynamoDB.

questions.stem: A DynamoDB table holds millions of support tickets. A small number are escalated and have an escalatedAt attribute; the rest do not have it. A dashboard must list escalated tickets efficiently. What should the developer do?

options.text: Scan the table with a filter on escalatedAt
options.rationale: The scan reads every ticket to return a few.

options.text: Add escalatedAt to every item, with a placeholder value such as N/A
options.rationale: This puts every item in an index on that attribute and loses the benefit of a sparse index.

options.text: Create a sparse GSI keyed on escalatedAt
options.rationale: Items without the index key are left out, so this sparse index contains only escalated tickets.

options.text: Query the table's partition key for the value escalated
options.rationale: The partition key is not the escalation status, so this query does not apply.

questions.explanation: A sparse index includes only items that have the index key, which makes it efficient for finding a small subset.
